title: Quantum Phase Transitions and Fractional Quantized Anomalous Hall Insulators in Rhombohedral Graphene
authors: Zach Hadjri, Xinlei Yue, Tonghang Han, Yuxuan Yao, Zhengguang Lu, Shenyong Ye, Junseok Seo, Jixiang Yang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Liang Fu, Ady Stern, Long Ju
abstract: Fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect (FQAHE) has been discovered in twisted MoTe$_2$ and rhombohedral graphene/hBN moiré superlattices. Such van der Waals heterostructures feature a tuning knob of gate displacement field $D$, which is absent from the conventional fractional quantum Hall systems in two-dimensional electron gases. $D$ plays a critical role in engineering FQAHE and other emergent quantum states and provides an exciting new opportunity to explore their quantum phase transitions. However, the microscopic details of such transitions and temperature-dependent transport have remained mostly elusive. Here we report systematic resistance measurements in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene/hBN moiré superlattices. We found that the displacement field-driven phase transitions between Composite Fermi liquid, Fermi liquid, Fractional Chern insulators, and insulating states are described by semi-circle relations of the longitudinal and transverse resistivities (or conductivities), largely unexplored in the fractional quantum Hall systems. This agrees with a spatially separated two-phase picture for the phase transitions and further indicates a new insulator phase--fractional quantized anomalous Hall insulator. By comparing the temperature-dependence of longitudinal resistance with the thermal activation model, we estimated the transport gap sizes in three fractional Chern insulator states. Our work shed light on the quantum and temperature evolutions of fractional Chern insulator states--providing necessary background for anyon-braiding and gate-defined junctions in rhombohedral graphene.
summary: This paper reports on transport measurements in graphene moiré superlattices to map out quantum phase transitions between various correlated electronic states. By analyzing the semi-circle behavior of resistivity and fitting temperature dependence, the authors confirm the existence of a fractional quantized anomalous Hall insulator phase. This work provides crucial experimental background for understanding topological quantum phenomena in tunable 2D materials.
main_problem: The study investigates quantum phase transitions and the nature of fractional quantized anomalous Hall insulators (FQAHI) in rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices.
main_result: Phase transitions between various correlated states (FL, FCI, CI) are characterized by semi-circle relations in resistivity/conductivity plots, confirming the existence of a new FQAHI phase.
method: Systematic resistance measurements, analysis of $ho_{xx}$ vs. $ho_{xy}$ semi-circle trajectories, and fitting temperature-dependent resistance data to thermal activation models.
model_or_system: The physical platform is rhombohedral pentalayer graphene/hBN moiré superlattices, which exhibit tunable quantum states controlled by a gate displacement field ($D$). The analysis uses the effective medium approximation for multi-phase transport.
key_observables: Longitudinal and transverse resistivities ($ho_{xx}, ho_{xy}$), temperature dependence of resistance, and semi-circle trajectories in the $ho_{xx}-ho_{xy}$ plane.
important_parameters:
Gate displacement field ($D$), temperature ($T$), and filling factors ($
u^*$) defining the different quantum phases.
main_assumptions: The use of the effective medium approximation for mixtures of phases, and the assumption that the phase fractions are determined by minimizing the free energy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate FL-FCI transitions via semi-circles, and show temperature-dependent transport analysis comparing thermal activation fits against $T^2$ metallic behavior for various fractional states.
paper_structure: The work systematically maps out phase transitions using transport measurements, employing the semi-circle law as a diagnostic tool, and then analyzes the temperature evolution of the insulating states using thermal activation models.
why_interesting: The study provides experimental evidence for highly correlated topological phases (FCI/FQAHI) in a tunable solid-state system, offering insights into emergent quantum behavior analogous to strongly correlated electron models.
